Received 2026-07-13, accepted 2026-08-05, published 2026-09-10 (PDF p. 1). The header and the citation box give pages 1166-1183, but the PDF on file has 17 pages numbered 1166-1182. The Resultados say the effect size is 'considerablemente mayor' than in earlier versions of this manuscript, possibly because of a transcription error in that earlier report (PDF p. 12).
source.title_on_document: Impacto de la Inteligencia Artificial Generativa sobre la Originalidad Creativa y el Pensamiento Proyectual en Estudiantes de Diseño Gráfico

supplement.where: None. The document mentions no supplementary material, annex, or online appendix. All statistics are in the main text (Tablas 3-6 and prose).

paper_design_summary: The study analyzed 96 graphic design students at one university in a control group and an experimental group of 48 each, formed from existing course sections (paralelos), not at random, which took the same eight-week course. Only the experimental group received generative AI training (week 2) and used ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL·E, and Adobe Firefly for research, ideation, and concept development (weeks 3 to 6). Two blinded external evaluators scored creative originality and design thinking with 1-5 analytic rubrics at pretest (week 1) and posttest (week 8), and the groups were compared by ANOVA on the posttest scores.

studies.label: Eight-week quasi-experiment in graphic design course sections (AI-supported vs conventional)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Generative AI training (week 2) and use of ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL·E, and Adobe Firefly (weeks 3 to 6), versus the same activities with conventional design strategies and no AI. The groups followed the existing course sections (paralelos), with a 1:1 split. The paper does not say how many sections formed each group.
assignment.quote: la asignación a los grupos control y experimental no fue aleatoria, sino determinada por los paralelos ya existentes de la asignatura, lo que corresponde a un diseño cuasi experimental
assignment.locator: PDF p. 15 (journal p. 1180), Limitaciones; also PDF p. 7 (p. 1172), Materiales y métodos: convenience sampling, 'manteniendo la organización natural de los grupos académicos'; PDF p. 8 (p. 1173), first phase: groups organized 1:1; PDF p. 14 (p. 1179), Discusión: 'sin aleatorización'

arms.name: Experimental
arms.description: Same course content, activities, learning objectives, and grading criteria as the control group, plus generative AI training (week 2) and use of ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL·E, and Adobe Firefly for research, ideation, generating alternatives, and concept development of the projects (weeks 3 to 6).

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Same course content, activities, learning objectives, and grading criteria, carried out with conventional design strategies, without AI assistance and without the AI training session.

participants.exclusions: Convenience sample. Inclusion required enrollment in the course, the corresponding academic level, signed informed consent, and at least 80 percent attendance at intervention sessions. Exclusion covered repeated absence during the intervention, dropping out, or incomplete evaluation instruments (PDF p. 7). The 96 are the students who met these criteria. The paper does not say how many students were excluded or how many were first placed in each group, and assignment was not random, so no randomized count exists. Tabla 6 gl (1, 94) match 96 analyzed.
participants.who: University students in the Graphic Design program (carrera de Diseño Gráfico), one course at one institution; 52 women (54.2 percent) and 44 men (45.8 percent); 60 aged 18-21 (62.5 percent) and 36 aged 22-25 (37.5 percent) (Tabla 4).
participants.country: Not stated for the sample, and the institution is not named. All author affiliations are in Ecuador (Universidad Internacional SEK, Quito; Universidad Nacional de Chimborazo, Riobamba).
participants.quote: La muestra quedó conformada por 96 estudiantes, distribuidos equitativamente en un grupo control (n = 48) y un grupo experimental (n = 48).
participants.locator: PDF p. 7 (journal p. 1172), Materiales y métodos; PDF pp. 10-11 (pp. 1175-1176), Tabla 4

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, Midjourney, DALL·E, Adobe Firefly (model versions not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: Use of one chatbot (ChatGPT) and three text-to-image tools (Midjourney, DALL·E, Adobe Firefly) as support for research, ideation, generating alternatives, and concept development of the course projects in weeks 3 to 6, after a training session in week 2 (Tabla 1 lists 'Ideación asistida por IA' in week 4). The paper does not describe limits on use or say which tool served which activity, so the role spans open_chat and image_generation and is coded other. AI use was recorded by self-report (PDF p. 15).

task.description: Graphic design course project: problem research, ideation, concept development, graphic proposals, and critical evaluation (Tabla 1). The rubrics scored creative originality and design thinking at pretest and posttest. The paper does not describe the pretest or posttest task. The Discusión says the rubric scoring centred on the visual originality and design coherence of 'las propuestas finales' (PDF p. 14).
task.duration: Eight weeks: pretest week 1, AI training week 2, AI use weeks 3-6, critical evaluation week 7, posttest and focus groups week 8 (Tabla 1, PDF p. 8)

outcomes.name: Creative originality (originalidad creativa), posttest rubric score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Analytic rubric with four dimensions, each scored 1-5: novelty (originality of the proposal), flexibility (diversity of solutions proposed), elaboration (development and refinement of the proposal), usefulness (relevance and functionality of the design solution) (Tabla 2, PDF p. 9). The paper uses 'originalidad creativa' as a short label for this composite creative performance (PDF p. 3), so the construct is overall creativity. Only the composite is reported. Scored double-blind by two external evaluators ('evaluadores externos', 'jueces externos') whose background is not described; expert_raters is provisional. ICC = .98, exact agreement 96.9 percent (PDF p. 9). Robustness: an ANCOVA with the pretest as covariate gave a group effect 'prácticamente idéntico' to the ANOVA, with no numbers printed (PDF p. 12).

contrasts.reported: Posttest M ± DE: Control 2.65 ± 0.45, Experimental 4.12 ± 0.58; n = 48 per group (Tabla 4). Pretest: Control 2.52 ± 0.40, Experimental 2.56 ± 0.44. ANOVA: F = 170.51, gl = 1, 94, p < .001, η² = 0.65. ANCOVA with pretest covariate: group effect 'prácticamente idéntico'; pretest did not predict posttest (p > .60); no other numbers. Pretest equivalence: Levene F = 0.05, p = .828; t = 0.18, p = .857; U de Mann–Whitney p = .812.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (journal p. 1176), Tabla 5 and pretest-equivalence paragraph; PDF p. 12 (p. 1177), Tabla 6 and ANCOVA paragraph; PDF pp. 10-11 (pp. 1175-1176), Tabla 4 (n per group)

outcomes.name: Design thinking (pensamiento proyectual), posttest rubric score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Design-process quality: analytic rubric with four dimensions, each scored 1-5: research (understanding of the problem and search for information), conceptualization (definition of the design concept), ideation (generation and exploration of alternatives), evaluation (justification and design decisions) (Tabla 2, PDF p. 9). Not a creativity construct in the codebook list, so coded other. Only the composite is reported. Same two blinded external evaluators, background not described; expert_raters is provisional. ICC = .94, exact agreement 90.6 percent (PDF p. 9). Robustness: the ANCOVA with the pretest as covariate gave a group effect 'prácticamente idéntico' to the ANOVA (PDF p. 12).

contrasts.reported: Posttest M ± DE: Control 2.58 ± 0.40, Experimental 4.05 ± 0.61; n = 48 per group (Tabla 4). Pretest: Control 2.45 ± 0.35, Experimental 2.51 ± 0.41. ANOVA: F = 186.57, gl = 1, 94, p < .001, η² = 0.67. ANCOVA with pretest covariate: group effect 'prácticamente idéntico'; pretest did not predict posttest (p > .60). Pretest equivalence: Levene F = 0.15, p = .696; t = −0.65, p = .515; U de Mann–Whitney p = .623.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (journal p. 1176), Tabla 5 and pretest-equivalence paragraph; PDF p. 12 (p. 1177), Tabla 6 and ANCOVA paragraph; PDF pp. 10-11 (pp. 1175-1176), Tabla 4 (n per group)

company_involvement.description: No company, funder, or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the document. All five authors list university affiliations.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 fails: the groups were the existing course sections, and the paper states that assignment was not random (PDF p. 15, Limitaciones; PDF p. 14, 'sin aleatorización'). The study analyzed 96 students (48 + 48; Tabla 6 gl 1, 94), well above 50, and both outcomes are rubric scores of the students' design work by two blinded external evaluators, so criteria 2 and 3 are met. As a non-random comparison of people working with and without AI (quasi_people), the study is observational context. The experimental group also received AI training that the control group did not (PDF p. 15).

one_line_finding: In a non-randomized comparison of two groups of graphic design students at one university (48 analyzed per group), the group that used generative AI scored higher at posttest on creative originality (4.12 vs 2.65 on a 1-5 rubric; F(1, 94) = 170.51, p < .001, η² = 0.65) and on design thinking (4.05 vs 2.58; F(1, 94) = 186.57, p < .001, η² = 0.67) (PDF pp. 11-12, Tablas 5-6).
open_questions: Whether AI was available when the scored posttest work was produced (with_ai or after_ai). The Tabla 1 note limits AI use to weeks 3-6, the posttest came in week 8 'utilizando los mismos instrumentos empleados durante la evaluación inicial', and the third phase promises 'condiciones equivalentes de aplicación' at pretest and posttest (PDF p. 8). These point to an unassisted posttest (after_ai, delayed). The Discusión says the rubric centred on 'las propuestas finales' after 'ocho semanas de apoyo generativo continuo' (PDF p. 14), which points to the AI-assisted project work (with_ai). The form keeps with_ai and yes, as screener B coded. The paper does not settle it.
The two raters are called 'evaluadores externos' and 'jueces externos', and their background is never described. Coded expert_raters provisionally.
The number of course sections (paralelos) per group is not stated, so the number of clusters cannot be assessed. The ANOVA treats the 96 students as independent.
The experimental group also received AI training in week 2 that the control group did not. The authors flag this confound (PDF p. 15).

Consistency flag for extraction, computed by the reconciler and not printed in the paper: a one-way ANOVA on the Tabla 5 posttest means and SDs with 48 per group gives F of about 192 (originality) and 195 (design thinking), and at least 186 and 189 after allowing for rounding. The printed F values, 170.51 and 186.57, are lower. The printed η² values (0.65, 0.67) are also slightly above F/(F + 94) for the printed F (0.64, 0.66). The paper says it verified the effect size from participant-level data and from Tabla 5 (PDF p. 12). The finalizer adds a check of the same kind: the Tabla 5 pretest means and SDs give an originality t of about 0.47 (0.35 to 0.59 after allowing for rounding), but the printed value is t = 0.18, p = .857 (PDF p. 11). The printed design-thinking pretest t = −0.65 fits within rounding (0.63 to 0.91). The form records the printed values.
The country and institution of the sample are not named. Ecuador is inferred only from the author affiliations.
notes: Locators give the PDF page (1-17) with the journal page in parentheses (journal page = PDF page + 1165). Mixed-methods paper with a sequential explanatory design. Tabla 3 (PDF p. 10) reports posttest Shapiro–Wilk and Levene checks only. A Spearman correlation between the two posttest outcomes (rho = .73, p < .001, PDF pp. 12-13) is not a treatment contrast and is not listed. Four focus groups (n = 24, 12 per condition, 45-60 minutes; PDF p. 9) produced themes including a 'riesgo latente de homogeneización estética' (PDF p. 13, Tabla 7), but no diversity outcome was measured. The data from the Likert instruments on generative AI and 'creatividad expandida' were lost, so the planned PLS-SEM was not run (PDF pp. 6, 15-16). No standard errors or confidence intervals are printed anywhere. The paper mentions no preregistration and gives no data or code links. Finalizer (2026-10-05): no challenge files exist for c056, because the finish-18 run ran the challenge step only for c075, c109, and c126 (RESUME.md), so final.challenge_resolution is empty and its counts are 0. The finalizer checked the form against the PDF instead. The header and dates (p. 1), Materiales y métodos with Tablas 1-2 (pp. 7-9), Tablas 3-6 with the pretest-equivalence and ANCOVA passages (pp. 10-12), and the later sections (pp. 13-16) match every recorded number, quote, and locator. A text search of all 17 pages found no supplement, funding, conflict-of-interest, data, or preregistration statement. Edits: 'analyzed' for the counts in paper_design_summary and one_line_finding (current spec); ai_tool.how_used no longer says 'free use', which the paper does not state; this note now says that the data from the Likert instruments were lost, as the paper says; open question 5 adds a pretest t check.

reconciliation.notes: This file replaces an earlier reconciliation (written 2026-10-05 09:18) of a previous pair of raw forms. The raw forms on disk were rewritten at 14:21 the same day, and this reconciliation uses them. Differences are counted per field and per outcome. Wording differences with the same meaning (for example, A listing three of the four inclusion criteria and B listing one) are not counted, and the final form lists all four.

open_items.item: AI availability while the scored posttest work was produced (open question 1; the unresolved reconciliation differences on ai_available_when_produced for S1-O1 and S1-O2). The form keeps with_ai, yes, and immediate, because the Discusión says the rubrics scored 'las propuestas finales' (PDF p. 14). The Tabla 1 note limits AI use to weeks 3-6, and the posttest came in week 8 (PDF p. 8), which would make both outcomes after_ai and delayed. The answer changes the question code, not eligibility: criterion 3 holds either way, and criterion 1 fails either way.

Background of the two external evaluators (open question 2; the unresolved reconciliation differences on measure for S1-O1 and S1-O2). expert_raters stays provisional. Criterion 3 accepts scoring by raters of any background, so only the measure code depends on it.

Number of course sections (paralelos) in each group (open question 3). It bears on clustering and standard errors (codebook Section 10), not on criterion 1, which fails because the paper states that assignment was not random.

AI training given only to the experimental group (open question 4). The paper states this confound itself (PDF p. 15), and the arms record training plus AI use against conventional work. No eligibility criterion depends on it.

Printed test statistics that do not fit Tabla 5 (open question 5): the posttest means and SDs give F of about 192 and 195 against the printed 170.51 and 186.57, and the printed pretest originality t = 0.18 is below the 0.35 to 0.59 that Tabla 5 allows. The form records the printed values. This matters for extraction, not eligibility.
Country and institution of the sample (open question 6). Neither is named, and Ecuador comes only from the author affiliations. This is descriptive metadata.
